title: Choosing without order
objectives: Count unordered selections and see why we divide by $r!$.
Tell a committee from a ranking.

screens.prose: Four analysts, Ana, Ben, Cal and Dev, want to go to a conference. The desk can send two of them. Both go as equals.
screens.question: How many different pairs could the desk send?

hints.text: List the pairs that include Ana.
Ana could go with Ben, Cal or Dev.
Ana gives 3 pairs. Ben gives 2 new ones, with Cal or Dev. Then Cal and Dev.

feedback.correct: Six pairs: AB, AC, AD, BC, BD and CD.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. List the pairs, and count Ana with Ben only once.

byKey.ordered: You counted Ana then Ben and Ben then Ana as different. They send the same two people.
byKey.square: You let an analyst pair with herself. A pair needs two different people.
byKey.four: You counted the analysts. Each pair is two of them together.
byKey.added: You added 4 and 4. Count the pairs themselves: AB, AC and so on.

explain.text: Ana pairs with 3 others, Ben with 2 new ones and Cal with 1 more: 6 pairs. Ana and Ben is the same pair as Ben and Ana. Next we link this to picking in order.

canvas.caption: AB, AC, AD, BC, BD, CD

screens.prose: Here the desk picks one analyst first and then a second. Each cell is an ordered pick: row B, column A means Ben first, then Ana. Nobody is picked twice, so the diagonal is greyed out.
screens.question: Tap both cells that send Ana and Ben.

hints.text: Ana and Ben can be picked in two orders.
Look in row A and in row B.

feedback.correct: AB and BA both send Ana and Ben.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find Ana then Ben, and Ben then Ana.

byKey.r2c1: You found Ana then Ben. Ben then Ana, in row B, sends the same two people.
byKey.r1c2: You found Ben then Ana. Ana then Ben, in row A, sends the same two people.

explain.text: The 12 cells off the diagonal are the ordered picks, $4 \times 3$. Every pair fills exactly two of them, one for each order. So there are $12 \div 2 = 6$ pairs.

screens.prose: A choice where order does not matter is a **combination**, also called a selection. We write $\binom{4}{2} = 6$, read 4 choose 2. You found it as ordered picks divided by 2. Now there are five analysts.
screens.question: What is $\binom{5}{2}$?

hints.text: How many cells are off the diagonal?
Five rows of 4 cells each.
20 ordered picks, each pair counted twice.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the ordered picks, then divide by the 2 orders of each pair.

byKey.ordered: You counted the ordered picks. Each pair fills two cells, so halve it.
byKey.square: You counted the diagonal too. Nobody can be picked twice.
byKey.five: You counted the analysts. Count the pairs.

explain.text: There are $5 \times 4 = 20$ ordered picks, and each pair appears twice. So $\binom{5}{2} = 20 \div 2 = 10$. The shaded cells hold each pair once.

screens.prose: Now pick 3 of 5 analysts for a risk committee. In order, that is $5 \times 4 \times 3 = 60$ picks. The committee shown is Ana, Ben and Cal.
screens.question: In how many of the 60 ordered picks does this same committee appear?

hints.text: In how many orders could Ana, Ben and Cal have been picked?
This is the number of ways to line up 3 people.
$3! = 3 \times 2 \times 1$.

feedback.correct: Three people can be picked in $3! = 6$ orders.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the orders of Ana, Ben and Cal.

byKey.three: You counted one order per member. Three people line up in $3 \times 2 \times 1$ ways.
byKey.two: You swapped just one pair, as with two people. Three people have $3! = 6$ orders.
byKey.one: The committee is one group, but it can be picked in several orders.

explain.text: ABC, ACB, BAC, BCA, CAB and CBA all give the same committee: $3! = 6$ orders. Every committee appears 6 times among the 60. So there are $60 \div 6 = 10$ committees.

screens.prose: Six analysts now, and the committee still has 3 seats. Divide the ordered picks by the orders of each committee.
screens.question: What is $\binom{6}{3}$?

hints.text: How many ordered picks of 3 from 6 are there?
$6 \times 5 \times 4 = 120$.
Each committee appears $3! = 6$ times among the 120.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count ordered picks, then divide by $3!$.

byKey.ordered: You counted ordered picks. Each committee appears 6 times among them.
byKey.by-three: You divided by 3. Three people have $3! = 6$ orders.
byKey.repeats: You let an analyst take two seats.

explain.text: $6 \times 5 \times 4 = 120$ ordered picks, and each committee appears $3! = 6$ times. So $\binom{6}{3} = 20$.

screens.prose: The desk sends 3 of 5 analysts to a conference. The other 2 stay in the office.
screens.question: How do $\binom{5}{3}$ and $\binom{5}{2}$ compare?

options.why: You expected a bigger group to give more choices. But every group that goes fixes the pair that stays.
You expected a smaller group to leave more freedom. But every pair that stays fixes the three who go.

hints.text: If you know who stays, do you know who goes?
The Stay box decides the Go box.
Each choice of 3 to go matches exactly one choice of 2 to stay.

feedback.correct: Choosing who goes is the same as choosing who stays.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pick the 2 who stay, and see what that settles.

explain.text: Choosing 3 to go is the same act as choosing 2 to stay. Each group of 3 matches exactly one pair left out, so $\binom{5}{3} = \binom{5}{2} = 10$. In general, $\binom{n}{r} = \binom{n}{n-r}$.

screens.prose: From 8 traders, a desk picks 3 for a risk committee. All three have equal votes. Sam writes $8 \times 7 \times 6 = 336$.
screens.question: How many committees are there?

options.why: That is Sam's answer. He counted ordered picks, as if first, second and third were different jobs. Each committee appears $3! = 6$ times.
You divided by 3, not by $3! = 6$. Three people have 6 orders.
You worked out $8^3$, which lets one trader take two seats.

hints.text: Do the 3 seats on the committee differ?
The members have equal votes, so the seats are the same.
Divide Sam's ordered count by the $3!$ orders of each committee.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether swapping two members gives a new committee.

byKey.ranked: You counted rankings, not committees. Swapping two members gives the same committee, so divide by $3!$.

explain.text: Sam's 336 counts each committee once for each of its $3! = 6$ orders. So there are $336 \div 6 = 56$ committees. If the seats were chair, deputy and secretary, 336 would be right.

canvas.caption: 2, 5, 7 is one committee, picked in 6 orders

screens.prose: Each time, you divided the ordered picks by the orders of the chosen group: $$\binom{n}{r} = \dfrac{P(n, r)}{r!} = \dfrac{n!}{r!\,(n-r)!}$$ Swapping $r$ and $n - r$ leaves the formula unchanged. That is the symmetry you saw with who goes and who stays.
screens.question: Which is equal to $\binom{10}{7}$?

options.why: You took 3 from the 7 chosen. The group is still drawn from all 10.
That is $10 \times 9 \times 8$, ordered picks of 3. It still needs dividing by $3!$.
You swapped the top and bottom. You cannot choose 10 from 7.

hints.text: Choosing 7 of 10 also decides how many are left out.
Picking 7 to go is picking 3 to stay.

feedback.correct: Choosing 7 of 10 is choosing the 3 left out: both are 120.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about who is left out.

explain.text: Choosing 7 of 10 is choosing the 3 left out. So $\binom{10}{7} = \binom{10}{3} = \dfrac{10 \times 9 \times 8}{3!} = 120$. The smaller one is quicker to work out.

screens.prose: We want to derive $\binom{n}{r} = \dfrac{n!}{r!\,(n-r)!}$ from what you know about ordered picks.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: Picking $r$ of $n$ in order gives $P(n, r) = \dfrac{n!}{(n-r)!}$ ordered picks.
The $r$ people in one group can be picked in $r!$ orders.
So the ordered picks fall into lots of $r!$, one lot for each group.

hints.text: Start from the count you already have.
Then ask how often each group is counted.
Ordered picks, orders of one group, the lots, then divide.

feedback.correct: Each group is counted $r!$ times, so divide by $r!$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from the ordered count and end by dividing.

byKey.divide: Dividing is the last step. First show that each group is counted $r!$ times.
byKey.grouped: The lots of $r!$ only make sense once you know a group has $r!$ orders.

explain.text: You started from ordered picks, then saw each group counted $r!$ times. Dividing removes the repeats. With $n = 6$ and $r = 3$: $\dfrac{720}{6 \times 6} = 20$, as you found.

screens.prose: A fund builds an equal-weighted portfolio of 3 stocks from a shortlist of 10. Each stock gets a third of the money, so the order of picking does not matter.
screens.question: How many different portfolios could the fund hold?

hints.text: Count ordered picks of 3 from 10 first.
$10 \times 9 \times 8 = 720$.
Each portfolio appears $3! = 6$ times among the 720.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count ordered picks, then divide by the orders of each portfolio.

byKey.ordered: You counted ordered picks. Equal weights mean the same three stocks make the same portfolio in any order.
byKey.repeats: You let one stock be picked twice.
byKey.by-three: You divided by 3. Three stocks have $3! = 6$ orders.
byKey.added: You added 10, 9 and 8. The picks multiply, then you divide.

explain.text: $\binom{10}{3} = \dfrac{10 \times 9 \times 8}{3!} = 120$. With weights of 50%, 30% and 20%, order would matter. Then there would be $P(10, 3) = 720$ portfolios.

canvas.caption: B, E, H is one of 120 portfolios

ideas: Ordered picks count each group once for every order of its members, which is $r!$ times.
So the number of groups is the ordered count divided by $r!$.
Choosing who is in is the same as choosing who is out: $\binom{n}{r} = \binom{n}{n-r}$.

formula.name: Combinations of r from n
formula.note: Also written ${}^{n}C_{r}$, the nCr key on a calculator. Read it as $n$ choose $r$.

summary.trap: A committee of equals is not a ranking. If swapping two members changes nothing, divide by $r!$.

quiz.prose: A stock is up or down on each of the 5 trading days of a week.
quiz.question: How many up-down patterns have exactly 2 up days?

options.why: You picked the two up days in order. Up on Monday and Tuesday is one pattern, however you pick it.
You counted every pattern of the week, $2^5$. Only some have exactly two up days.
You let the same day be picked twice.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Choose which 2 of the 5 days are up.

explain.text: A pattern is fixed by which 2 days are up. So there are $\binom{5}{2} = \dfrac{5 \times 4}{2} = 10$ patterns.

quiz.prose: A manager has a shortlist of 7 stocks and decides to hold all of them.
quiz.question: In how many ways can she choose the 7 stocks to hold?

options.why: You counted the stocks. There is only one group of all seven.
That is $7!$, the orders of the seven. A portfolio of all seven has no order.
You read no choice as no ways. Taking all of them is one way.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. How many different groups of all seven are there?

explain.text: There is one group that holds all seven: $\binom{7}{7} = \dfrac{7!}{7!\,0!} = 1$. By symmetry it matches $\binom{7}{0} = 1$, the one way to hold nothing.

quiz.prose: A desk picks 9 of its 12 traders for an offsite. There is a quick way to work this out.
quiz.question: How many groups of 9 could it pick? This is $\binom{12}{9}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Choose the 3 left out instead.

byKey.ordered: You found $12 \times 11 \times 10$, ordered picks of 3. Divide by $3!$.
byKey.half: You divided by 2. Three left out have $3! = 6$ orders.
byKey.product: You multiplied 12 by 9. Choose the 3 left out and use the formula.

explain.text: Choosing 9 of 12 is choosing the 3 left out. So $\binom{12}{9} = \binom{12}{3} = \dfrac{12 \times 11 \times 10}{6} = 220$.

quiz.prose: From 6 traders, a desk names a chair and a deputy chair for its risk meeting.
quiz.question: In how many ways can the two roles be filled?

options.why: You counted pairs. Chair and deputy are different jobs, so Ana as chair with Ben as deputy differs from the swap.
You let one trader hold both roles: $6 \times 6 = 36$.
You added 6 and 5. The two roles are stages, so multiply.

feedback.correct: $6 \times 5 = 30$: the roles differ, so order matters.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Do the two roles differ?

explain.text: The roles differ, so this is a permutation: $P(6, 2) = 6 \times 5 = 30$. A pair of equal members would be $\binom{6}{2} = 15$.
